name: SuperDisplay
subcategory: second screen / tablet as external display
tagline: Turns an Android tablet into a real second monitor for a Windows PC over USB or Wi-Fi, with pen and touch input.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: This looks like a screen sharing app and is actually a display driver. The hard part is a signed Windows indirect display driver that makes the OS believe a second monitor exists, with correct resolution, scaling, hotplug and sleep behavior, then a capture and encode pipeline that holds latency low enough that dragging a window does not feel like a video call. An agent can absolutely build you a LAN mirror in a browser tab, and it will work, and it will feel wrong the first time you try to draw on it. Driver signing alone puts a real one-shot out of reach: unsigned drivers need test signing mode or a kernel policy you probably do not want on your daily machine. The consolation build is useful for glanceable panels, Slack, docs, logs, not for pen work.
coreLoopDIY: Creates a virtual second display on Windows, captures it, streams H.264 to a browser on the tablet over LAN, and injects touch events back as mouse input.
requirements: Windows 11 PC with a GPU that supports hardware H.264 encode
An existing open source indirect display driver (IddSampleDriver or similar) plus test signing mode enabled, or you only get mirroring of an existing screen
Tablet and PC on the same LAN, ideally wired or 5 GHz
Comfort with Windows driver install, certificates and the occasional blue screen
whatYouLose: Sub-20ms latency: a browser MSE pipeline lands in the hundreds of milliseconds and pen input feels detached
Pressure sensitivity and palm rejection for stylus work
USB transport, so you are hostage to Wi-Fi quality and battery drain
Correct DPI, rotation, hotplug and resume-from-sleep behavior, the stuff you only notice when it breaks
A signed driver that installs on a normal machine without disabling security features
moatNotes: The moat is not an algorithm, it is a thousand small correctness fixes in a layer of Windows that nobody enjoys working in.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the alternative is a real external monitor or a bad experience, and the price of this thing is somewhere between a coffee and a cheap lunch. People pay to not care about the driver signing, the codec negotiation, the DPI math and the tablet going to sleep mid-session. That is the entire value proposition, and it is a fair one.
notes: A browser mirror over LAN gets you most of the pixels and none of the feel. The moat is the signed indirect display driver and a millisecond budget that makes a tablet behave like glass instead of a video stream.
prompt:
Build a LAN second-screen tool for Windows 11 called "panelcast". Two parts in one repo: a C# .NET 8 console host that runs on the PC, and a single static HTML page served by that host that the tablet opens in Chrome.

Stack, no alternatives: C# .NET 8, Vortice.Windows for DXGI Desktop Duplication, ffmpeg invoked as a child process for H.264 encoding, ASP.NET Core minimal API with a WebSocket endpoint, vanilla JS plus Media Source Extensions on the client. No Electron, no React, no cloud, no accounts, no telemetry.

Host behavior:
1. Enumerate displays on startup and let the user pick one by index with a --display flag, default 0. Print the list and exit if --list is passed.
2. Capture the chosen display with Desktop Duplication at up to 60 fps, skipping frames when nothing changed.
3. Pipe raw BGRA frames to ffmpeg: h264_nvenc if available, fall back to libx264 with preset ultrafast and tune zerolatency, output fragmented MP4 to stdout with movflags frag_keyframe+empty_moov+default_base_moof and a short GOP.
4. Push each fMP4 fragment to connected WebSocket clients as a binary message. Drop fragments for clients whose send buffer is backed up rather than queueing.
5. Accept JSON input messages on the same socket: {type:"move",x,y}, {type:"down",button}, {type:"up",button}, {type:"scroll",dy}. x and y are 0..1 normalized to the captured display. Inject them with SendInput via P/Invoke, mapping to absolute virtual desktop coordinates for the correct monitor. Gate all input injection behind a --input flag that defaults to off.
6. Bind to 0.0.0.0 on a port from .env (PORT), require a shared token from .env (ACCESS_TOKEN) as a query param on the WebSocket and on the page. Read .env with no dependency beyond a 20 line parser. Ship .env.example, never a real secret.

Client page: full screen black, canvas-free, a single video element fed by MSE, pointer events forwarded as the messages above, a tap-to-fullscreen prompt, and a visible latency estimate based on fragment arrival timing. Nothing else.

Explicitly out of scope, do not attempt: writing or installing a display driver, code signing, stylus pressure, USB transport, audio, multi-monitor cloning, auto-discovery. If the user wants an actual extra desktop rather than a mirror of an existing one, the README tells them to install a third party indirect display driver separately and then point --display at it.

Deliverables: README with exact run commands, .env.example, and a honest LIMITATIONS section that states measured latency is roughly 150 to 400 ms and that this is not suitable for drawing.
